title: Shakespeare and the Classics
author: Leithart, Peter
summary: Peter Leithart examines Shakespeare's relationship to ancient Greek civilization, correcting the modern assumption that the Renaissance and medieval periods viewed Greece as the fountainhead of Western culture the way we do today. He notes that medievals knew Greek literature only through Latin translation and that Elizabethans, like their medieval forebears, felt closer kinship to Rome than to Greece — true classical Greek scholarship as a discipline did not emerge until the eighteenth century. Still, Leithart traces a genuine Renaissance revival of interest in Greece: a wave of translations (Chapman's Iliad and Odyssey, partial Herodotus, Thucydides, Plato, and Aristotle), a renewed dramatic tradition following the medieval eclipse of classical theater, and Shakespeare's own choice to set several plays in Greek settings (Venus and Adonis, Timon of Athens, A Midsummer Night's Dream, Troilus and Cressida, and Pericles). He observes that Shakespeare's direct dramatic influences were more Roman than Greek, but that Troilus and Cressida offers a window into how Shakespeare assessed the Greek heroic world and its values.
points: Corrects the modern assumption that Greece has always been seen as the fountainhead of Western civilization — medievals and Elizabethans saw Rome, not Greece, as their nearer ancestor.
Notes that classical Greek scholarship as a formal discipline is an 18th-century invention, per David Gress, that functioned almost as an 'ersatz religion.'
Documents the Renaissance 'age of translation' that brought Homer, Herodotus, Thucydides, Plato, and Aristotle into English for the first time.

Identifies Shakespeare's Greek-set plays (Venus and Adonis, Timon of Athens, A Midsummer Night's Dream, Troilus and Cressida, Pericles) while noting his dramatic technique owed more to Roman than Greek models.
Uses Troilus and Cressida as evidence of Shakespeare's own critical assessment of the Greek heroic ethos and its values.
quotes: Today, many view ancient Greece, and especially ancient Athens, as the fountainhead of Western civilization. This was not the case for medievals, who knew Greek literature in Latin translations.

As David Gress says (in From Plato to NATO), classical scholarship was born in the eighteenth century, and took root in England and especially Germany as an "ersatz religion" and a "replacement for Christianity.
In 1611, George Chapman (made famous by Keats's poem) produced the first complete English translation of the Iliad taken from the Greek, and by 1614 had produced a translation of the Odyssey.

During the Middle Ages, Greek and Roman drama fell into obscurity, and a wholly new dramatic tradition grew up around liturgical events of the medieval church. During the Renaissance, classical drama was revived, and classically-influenced theaters were built.
The specific influences on Shakespeare were more from Roman drama than from Greek, however.
Still, Shakespeare's portrayal of the Greek heroic world and its values in Troilus and Cressida does give us some insight into his assessment of that world and those values.
